cards.title: Define Lifetime Gross Profit with a Time Constraint
cards.summary: Calculate LTGP as revenue minus COGS, delivery, fees and refunds, always anchored to a fixed window like 30/90/180 days.
cards.use_when: Deciding how much you can afford to pay for new customers, or setting the retention and LTV targets your store will be managed against.
steps: Replace the vague word LTV with LTGP (lifetime gross profit). Subtract from revenue: COGS, cost of delivery (shipping, 3PL/handling/pick-pack), transaction fees, and refunds. Refunds frequently belong here rather than in CAC.
Always attach a time constraint: 30-day LTGP, 90-day LTGP, 180-day LTGP. A raw 'lifetime' number spanning decades is unmeasurable and irrelevant to cash needs.

Build the cohort view by measuring the cumulative gross profit of each acquisition cohort at 30, 60, 90, 180 and 365 days. A customer might be worth $60 gross profit on day 0 and grow to $100 by day 90.

Calculate from real order-level data (e.g., Shopify order and refund line items) rather than assuming AOV x margin. Starting AOV and margin move around, especially during discount periods, so refresh at least monthly.
Use the constrained LTGP as the input to CAC targets and to KPI retention programs; ignore abstract lifetime revenue claims.
caveats: LTGP is a gross-profit-profit concept, not the software notion of LTV where revenue and gross profit roughly coincide. Comparing ecommerce LTGP to SaaS-style LTV will mislead.
Source is explicit that refunds should not be folded into CAC — doing so corrupts paid media signals — but must be captured in LTGP.

cards.title: Prioritize the Retention Hierarchy Before Touching Email and SMS
cards.summary: Fix product quality, product portfolio, acquisition quality and customer experience before expecting owned media to rescue retention.
cards.use_when: Repeat purchase rate or 90-day LTV is flat and you're tempted to invest in more email flows, SMS or Klaviyo work as the first fix.
steps: Work the hierarchy top-down, not bottom-up: 1) product quality, 2) product portfolio (natural cross-sell, upsell, replenishment), 3) acquisition quality, 4) customer experience across all touchpoints, 5) owned media (email, SMS, direct mail, WhatsApp).
Audit product quality using real customer evidence — surveys, NPS, verbatim feedback from buyers — not the founder's own view.

Check the portfolio for natural repurchase mechanics: is there a reason a customer must come back? If not, the fix may be a new product, collection, cross-sell or subscription rather than more messaging.

Examine acquisition quality: low-AOV TikTok Shop buyers and Black Friday 40-50% flash-sale bargain hunters repeat far less than a customer who spent $200 on the first order. First-order behavior is a strong predictor of retention.
Review the full customer experience, including post-purchase communication, shipping updates and support. A problem handled well can drive return rather than defection.
Only after the four foundations are healthy should you spend on owned media, where it acts as the amplifier that can exploit the constraint.
caveats: This is the source's stated hierarchy and opinion; it is not a universal law, and brands with a strong product may still get quick wins from flows.
Owned media can genuinely amplify retention once foundations are sound — the caution is about using it to mask a broken product or portfolio.

cards.title: Set a CAC Target from LTGP and an Efficiency Ratio
cards.summary: Divide the chosen LTGP window by a target LTGP:CAC ratio (2-3 for scaling) to get your CAC ceiling.
cards.use_when: Setting paid media bid and budget ceilings, or judging whether current CAC is efficient for your store's growth appetite.
steps: Choose the LTGP window you'll manage against. The source recommends 30-day LTGP for most stores; 90-day for CPG, supplements or high-repeat categories.

Pick a target LTGP:CAC ratio. The source's bands: sub-1 is losing money; 1-2 is inefficient but can work with strong working capital or an exit strategy; 2-3 is the scaling band; 3+ is leaving money on the table.
Divide the chosen LTGP by that ratio. Example: $80 30-day LTGP / 2 = $40 CAC target. Or $100 90-day LTGP / 2 = $50 CAC target.
Notice the effect of the window: moving from 30-day to 90-day in the example raised the CAC ceiling 25%, which can let you buy more customers if the extra volume is real.

Forecast the trade-off before committing: model new-customer acquisition volume against the higher CAC ceiling. If raising CAC by $10 only adds a small number of customers, stay conservative and profitable on first purchase.
Recalculate as cohorts mature; LTV bases are stable in growth rate but shift in starting point, especially around discounting.
caveats: Ratio bands are the source's heuristics, not a calculated law. 1-2 can be legitimately targeted by capital-rich brands aiming at a fast exit.
30-day LTGP as the standard is the source's recommendation for operators below roughly $15-20M, not a universal rule.

cards.title: Calculate the Mathematical Floor for CAC
cards.summary: CAC = CPC / conversion rate; use best realistic CPC and conversion rate to find the cheapest CAC you could ever achieve.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to invest in more paid media efficiency or in retention and LTV instead, or sanity-checking an over-optimistic CAC forecast.
steps: Use the identity CAC = CPC / conversion rate. Break it into the best realistic CPC and the best realistic conversion rate for your store.
Set the optimistic floor: source example uses $0.70 CPC / 3% conversion = $23 CAC — the best case the brand could ever reach.
Set the realistic case: source example uses $1.00 CPC / 2% conversion = $50 CAC, given the brand's actual performance and traffic quality.

Compare the floor vs. realistic CAC. The gap is the size of the paid-media opportunity. If the floor is far below current, there's room; if not, further CAC reduction is limited and LTV becomes the lever.
Use these bounds alongside a separate ceiling model for LTGP (offer restructuring, bundles, front-end offer tests, subscription strategy) to decide where to invest.
caveats: CPC is described as a fairly vanity metric that isn't strongly correlated with performance except at the extremes; very low CPC often means terrible traffic.
The 3% conversion and $0.70 CPC values are the source's worked example, not benchmarks to copy onto any store.

cards.title: Use CAC Payback Period for Subscription-first Brands
cards.summary: When first-purchase gross profit is below CAC, track the point at which cumulative subscription or replenishment profit repays the deficit.
cards.use_when: Running a supplements, CPG or subscription store that knowingly loses money on the first order.
steps: Accept the Day 0 loss explicitly. Example: $50 CAC vs $45 first-order gross profit = negative $5 contribution.
Track the CAC payback period: the date at which cumulative gross profit from the cohort crosses the initial deficit and the brand starts earning profit.
Drive it with retention levers — subscription depth, replenishment cadence, second/third purchase rates — because every additional repeat inside the payback window shortens the period.
Use the payback period as a standing KPI on the finance dashboard alongside contribution margin, since it directly ties retention tactics to how fast cash returns.
Before scaling, model how much capital you can afford to have tied up while cohorts are in the red — payback is a working capital constraint as much as a profit one.
caveats: The specific $50/$45 figures are an illustrative example, not a benchmark.
Requires a category with high repeat rate and natural replenishment; this framework does not fit one-off or durable-goods purchases.

cards.title: Decide the LTGP Window by Growth Appetite and Capital
cards.summary: Extend the payback window (30 to 90 to 180 days) only when you have the capital to fund losses on new customers and the modelling skill to manage it.
cards.use_when: Choosing whether to fund aggressive paid acquisition now by allowing a longer payback, or to stay conservative and cash-positive on first purchase.
steps: Match your window to funding model: bootstrapped or profit-first stores should anchor on 30-day LTGP; funded or capital-rich stores can push to 90 or 180 days.

Count the real risk of the aggressive model. The source notes loans require sophisticated financial modelling incorporating interest payments, and running that model well below roughly $15-20M annual revenue is very risky.

Model the volume response, not just the payback: if increasing the CAC ceiling by $10 buys meaningfully more customers (e.g., 30-40% more), extending the window can grow the business materially; if it barely moves volume, stay conservative.
Accept that going colder always raises CAC due to diminishing returns — the point of extending the window is to profit from the extra volume over time, not to pretend CAC will come back down.
Re-evaluate the window periodically as cash position, working capital and retention performance change.
caveats: These thresholds are the source's stated operator guidance, not tested benchmarks; individual risk tolerance and lender terms differ.
Extending the window increases the amount of cash locked in acquisition before it returns; a payback extension is not free.

cards.title: Stop Measuring Returning Customer % and Repeat Rate Confusion
cards.summary: Shopify's percentage of returning customers is orders-based and rises when acquisition weakens, so it's a poor LTV performance metric.
cards.use_when: Reviewing your store's repeat purchase health in Shopify analytics or recommending retention improvements based on that dashboard.
steps: Recognize that 'percentage of returning customer orders' equals returning customer orders / total orders, which is not the repeat rate.

Understand its two dominant drivers. Business age: a 15-year-old business naturally has a large returning base and this number trails upward with maturity. Acquisition strength: acquiring fewer first-time customers improves the ratio.
Because the metric improves when acquisition deteriorates, it incentivizes the wrong behaviour if used as a retention KPI.
Use it only for slicing sales-period analytics, e.g., seeing how a promotion resonated with new vs existing customers. Do not use it to judge LTV performance.
For actual repeat measurement, track first-to-second order conversion and cohort-based LTGP windows instead.
caveats: The source is definite that the metric is 'terrible' for indexing LTV, calling it a source opinion; it still has narrow diagnostic use during sale periods.
Exact Shopify dashboard availability and layout may change — verify the current interface.

cards.title: Inspect Which Half of the LTGP:CAC Ratio to Work On
cards.summary: CAC has a hard floor and LTGP a practical ceiling; estimate both first, then invest in the side with real headroom.
cards.use_when: Choosing between funding more paid media optimisation or funding retention, offer, bundle and subscription programs.
steps: Estimate the CAC floor using your best realistic CPC and highest realistic conversion rate (see the CAC floor calculation).
Estimate the LTGP ceiling using the strategies actually available to you: bundle restructuring, front-end offer tests, subscription strategy, retention programs within 90-365 days.
Compare headroom on each side. Inexperienced operators typically overestimate how low CAC can go and underestimate how high LTGP can be pushed.

Fund the side with more genuine headroom. If paid media is near its floor, retention, offer design and subscription work become the leverage; if retention is already strong, paid efficiency still matters.
Revisit the exercise at least quarterly — both floors and ceilings shift as creative, media buying, offers and retention improve.
caveats: CAC can only go so low before traffic quality degrades; do not assume continuous CAC reduction is achievable.
This is presented as a framework for thinking about the ratio, not a formula with fixed inputs.

cards.title: Balance Attribution and Profitability Metrics in Your Owned Media KPIs
cards.summary: Use Klaviyo attribution as a north-star indicator but drive day-to-day decisions from profitability metrics — and avoid the two extremes.
cards.use_when: Setting the reporting dashboard for your email/SMS retention program, or deciding what changes your retention team should make.
steps: Treat platform attribution metrics (account/campaign/flow attributed revenue, revenue per recipient, 30-50% revenue share from email) as an indicator only. They show whether you're reaching enough people, whether flows exist and whether cadence is sensible.

Take attribution with a grain of salt: outside studies cited by the source suggest roughly 70-80% of campaign revenue may be incremental for some accounts, but it varies heavily by brand. Bigger brands can run incrementality tests.
Balance with profitability metrics: LTGP adjusted for 90 and 365 days, mapped at 30/60/90/180/365 day cohorts, plus revenue from the top 20% of customers.

Avoid both extremes: chasing attribution alone means you optimise for looking good in dashboards; ignoring incremental repeat-revenue work in favour of pure long-term LTV means you never improve today's numbers.
Use attribution as the north star and profitability metrics as the constraint-finding tool that sets your retention targets.
caveats: The 30-50% revenue share figure is described as a soft indicator, not hard science.
Attribution and metric availability may change — verify current Klaviyo interface before building dashboards.

cards.title: Focus on Pop-up Conversion Rather Than Opt-in Rate
cards.summary: Judge pop-ups by the AOV, gross profit and conversion rate of signed-up customers, not by the opt-in percentage.
cards.use_when: Designing or reviewing a signup pop-up and deciding whether the captured audience is worth making new-customer content for.
steps: Stop treating a 5% or 10% opt-in rate as the target because someone said so; it says nothing about value.
Measure pop-up conversion: how many of the people who sign up actually purchase.
Measure the AOV and gross profit of customers who came through the pop-up, so you know what they are worth to the business.
Compare the value of this audience against other acquisition sources; a high-volume, low-value pop-up cohort may be less useful than a smaller, high-intent one.
Adjust the pop-up offer and experience based on those values, not on opt-in volume.
caveats: Pop-up conversion rate and AOV will differ widely by category; no universal target is provided.
The source treats opt-in rate as a vanity metric for this decision — attribution from pop-ups should be checked against profitability.

cards.title: Map the Customer Journey as F1/F2/F3 Functions and Structure Flows Around It
cards.summary: Organize every flow into acquisition, first-to-second order conversion, and top-20% loyalty stages so you can isolate and fix any constraint.
cards.use_when: Restructuring your Klaviyo account or asking 'where do I go to fix' when repeat purchase or LTV underperforms.
steps: Define F1 = acquisition, F2 = first-to-second order conversion, F3 = revenue from the top 20% of customers adjusted for gross profit. F stands for function, not phase, in the source's framing.

Map every flow trigger's first split to customer stage: new, returning, and loyal or subscription. New customers get trust and brand-introduction messaging, returning customers skip introductions and go straight to need, loyal/subscription customers get the least aggressive messaging and ideally no incentive.
Resist building flows that are one linear sequence for every entrant, or flows split first by product (denim vs t-shirt). Product splits are low-leverage compared to customer stage.
Because F2 correlates with 90-day LTGP and F3 with 365-day LTGP, you can identify which journey stage is your constraint and walk directly to the matching branches across all flows.
Once stage-based splitting is in place, layer optional splits (cart value tiers, product interest, win-back timing) as tests, not as the first structure.
Treat flows as the 24/7 engine where journey communication lives; campaigns are one-time sends. The source says the campaign-vs-flow revenue split matters less than this structure.
caveats: The source says the campaign vs flow revenue split is month-dependent and should not be a fixed target.
Product-based splits can still be tested later; they are not wrong, just not the starting point.
This is the source's framing; the specific email sequences and triggers belong to a separate email/SMS workflow and are not covered here.

cards.title: Segment Campaigns for Reach, Not Hyperpersonalization
cards.summary: Send elite content to as many engaged people as possible most of the time; reserve narrow segments for specific goals.
cards.use_when: Planning campaign sends and choosing whether to slice your email/SMS list into niche audiences.
steps: Adopt roughly 80/20 by source rule of thumb: 80% of the time focus on reach and top/middle-of-funnel content (education, entertainment, social proof, reviews) sent to the engaged base; 20% of the time execute specific-goal segments.

Grow the engaged audience segment using opens or clicks plus on-site actions (add-to-cart, checkout started, placed order) within windows you choose — the source uses examples like 180, 220 and 280 days based on the brand's cycle.
Define a target that at least 50% of the list falls into the engaged segment by default, and track the segment size growing over time.
For the 20% specific-goal sends, use them for things like excess stock on a brand, a supplier-led national sale, or a product-specific push — one clear business reason.
Build the 80/20 cadence on the compound value of elite content sent repeatedly: it protects deliverability, keeps baseline revenue up and makes sale peaks bigger.
Assess campaign success through year-on-year growth of the channel relative to the whole business, plus profitability metrics, not per-send revenue.
caveats: The 80/20 split and 50% engaged-share target are the source's rules of thumb, not universal benchmarks.
Hyperpersonalised niche segments still have some use for specific business goals, but the source found labour-to-upside rarely worth it at scale.

cards.title: Reclaim Suppressed Email Profiles before Big Campaign Moments
cards.summary: A 9-figure retailer was only reaching around 200k of 750k profiles; fixing the engaged-audience structure meant campaign peaks could reach far more people.
cards.use_when: Planning a sale, launch or restock and wondering how much of the email list will actually receive the message.
steps: Audit actual send sizes for recent campaigns and compare with total list size. In the source's case study of a 9-figure activewear retailer, campaigns were capped at around 50,000-200,000 of a 750,000 list.
Identify the deficit — the 550,000 profiles receiving almost nothing while you keep paying for them. Personalised small sends had consumed the team's energy without building a broad, engaged base.
Restructure around an engaged-audience definition (opens/clicks plus on-site events within defined windows) so campaigns can go to a broad, healthy segment for most sends.
Keep narrow segments for specific-goal moments (excess stock, brand-specific sales) rather than as the default.
Measure success by healthier deliverability, larger engaged audience over time and bigger revenue peaks during sale periods.
caveats: The 750,000 / 200,000 figures are case-study examples, not benchmarks.
The engaged-audience windows the source used (180/220/280 days) are business-specific; choose based on your purchase cycle.

cards.title: Plan Lifecycle Cohorts by Purchase and Subscription Stage
cards.summary: Map customers into never-purchased, purchased-but-not-subscribed, active subscriber and cancelled subscriber cohorts to set clear per-cohort goals.
cards.use_when: Designing retention strategy for a subscription or replenishment store and deciding what each part of the customer base should receive.
steps: Define the cohorts: never purchased, purchased but not subscribed, active subscribers, cancelled subscribers.

Assign a specific outcome to each cohort: never purchased → first sale, ideally onto subscription; purchased not subscribed → upsell into subscription or next purchase; active subscribers → retention/relationship protection; cancelled subscribers → reactivation.
Map this mapping into your customer journey and flow structure so each cohort's messaging matches its stage and value.
For non-subscription brands, substitute RFM analysis or loyalty tiers ($500+, $1,000+, $3,000+) to achieve the same clear cohort-based goals.
Use these cohorts to define what messages you'd stop sending — e.g., don't incentivise active subscribers, don't re-introduce the brand to a repeat buyer.
caveats: The source warns against hyper-segmenting campaigns by these cohorts; use them for strategy and journey planning, not as a mandate for every send.
Subscription cohort definitions may need adjustment by business model.

cards.title: Test Structure, Offers and Messaging — Not Subject Lines and Timings
cards.summary: A/B testing should target the identified constraint with structural, offer or messaging changes rather than cosmetic email optimisation.
cards.use_when: Directing a retention team's testing roadmap, or asking what to test after the email flows have been built.
steps: Set the testing agenda from the constraint identified in the F1/F2/F3 journey. If the constraint is first-to-second order conversion, test only things that can plausibly move that.

Prioritise three testing categories: 1) structure and timing — flow architecture, split order, campaign cadence, segmentation, time of day, flow delays; 2) offers — incentive size, structure, conditions, timing relative to stage; 3) messaging — copy, angles, headlines, creative.
Stop spending the test budget on subject lines, click-through rates and time delays as the main tests. The source frames that as 'being an email marketer' rather than a retention marketer.
Keep one person focused on high-level retention strategy and profitability, alongside executors who handle creative, subject lines and segmentation — both roles are needed.
Review success through 90/365-day LTGP, first-to-second conversion and top-customer revenue, not through in-platform opens or clicks.
caveats: Subject line and content tests are legitimate parts of an email marketer's job; the source's point is about prioritisation, not abolishing them.
Constraint-first testing requires first building the F1/F2/F3 structure, otherwise you cannot isolate where to test.

cards.title: Map Campaign Revenue to Calendar Peaks and Engagement Build
cards.summary: Repeat customer revenue arrives as waves tied to sales, launches and restocks, so year-round audience engagement is what creates the peaks.
cards.use_when: Planning your campaign calendar and deciding how much to invest in engagement-building content outside of sale periods.
steps: Separate new-customer revenue, which ideally climbs in a straight line, from repeat revenue, which comes in peaks and troughs.
Identify the events that create repeat-revenue peaks: sales periods, new products, restocks, and general marketing moments that give people a reason to buy.
Accept that peaks only cash in if a large, engaged audience was built during the quieter periods; invest in elite content consistently for a rising baseline.
Plan the year in two layers: always-on engagement content for the base, and event-based campaigns for the peaks.
Measure success year-on-year on the owned-media channel's share of revenue, not on any single send.
caveats: The source does not give a numeric percentage for peak uplift; do not assume fixed uplift from any campaign type.
This is a strategy model, not a measurement framework.

cards.title: Measure Retention at 30/60/90/180/365 Day Cohorts and Top-20% Revenue
cards.summary: Track LTGP-adjusted cohort curves by time window and revenue from the top 20% of customers to find where retention is lagging.
cards.use_when: Building a retention dashboard or answering 'is our retention programme actually working' with real numbers.
steps: Produce a cohort view of LTGP adjusted at 30, 60, 90, 180 and 365 days, using order-level data with refunds included.
Track the size and value of the top 20% of customers by spend — this indicates long-term loyalty and whether the retention programme is serving the highest-value segment.
Map the 90-day LTGP to the F2 (first-to-second order) function and 365-day LTGP to the F3 (loyalty) function so metrics attach to journey stages.
Use first-to-second order conversion as the primary F2 measurement because it is directly measurable, not inferred.
Analyse the cohort curves to locate the constraint, then direct structural tests at that stage.
caveats: The 30/60/90/180/365 day windows are the source's measurement choice, matching its LTGP windows, not a universal standard.
Top-20% revenue is a source indicator, not an owned KPI definition that will fit every brand.

cards.title: Recognize Why 80% of Most Brands' Customers Never Buy Twice
cards.summary: Sustained second-purchase failure usually traces to unaddressed retention foundations and the absence of a mapped customer journey.
cards.use_when: Interpreting a poor repeat purchase rate and deciding whether the issue is execution (emails) or foundations (product, portfolio, acquisition, experience).
steps: Assume the 80/20 non-repeat pattern is often a foundations problem before blaming messaging. Review the retention hierarchy top-down.
Check acquisition quality, since bargain-hunting and low-AOV acquisition channels predict lower repeat behaviour.
Check the product portfolio for natural cross-sell, upsell or replenishment. Without a reason to return, no flow will fix the number.
Confirm the customer journey is mapped into your account as new/returning/loyal paths; without that structure, you cannot even isolate the constraint.
Look at whether the store is misreading signals: e.g., relying on attribution dashboards and returning-customer percentage that improve when acquisition gets worse.
caveats: The 80% figure comes from the source's framing that only around 20% of customers buy a second time from most brands; treat it as an observed pattern rather than a hard benchmark.
Not every brand is in the same category — repeat rates differ widely between CPG, fashion and one-off products.

cards.title: Plan a Bundled, Subscription-first Offer Structure to Raise LTGP
cards.summary: Restructure bundles, front-end offers and subscription options to lift the LTGP ceiling within a 90-365 day window.
cards.use_when: Working the LTGP side of the LTGP:CAC ratio instead of pushing further on paid efficiency.
steps: Map the current LTGP ceiling within 90 and 365 days, including return purchase behaviour and subscription attach.
Identify bundles that increase AOV and starting gross profit without requiring heavier paid spend — e.g., multi-month packs, starter kits with replenishment.
Test new front-end offers with different structures (one-time vs subscribe-and-save, trial vs full-size) and measure their cohort LTGP, not first-order AOV alone.
Use subscription design to convert higher proportions of first-time buyers, and treat the subscription cohort's retention and cancellation events as leading LTV indicators.
Compare the LTGP uplift from each change against the effort and margin cost, and re-run the LTGP:CAC ratio to confirm extra paid headroom.
caveats: Offer and bundle design must be balanced against margin compression; the source notes discount periods reduce starting LTGP and CAC targets must be adjusted.
No specific uplift figures are provided; treat any change as a test to be measured on cohort data.
